articles.title: New insight brief offers reflections on what is needed from shipping’s regulatory enforcement mechanism
articles.summary: In the run-up to the 23rd Intersessional Working Group (ISWG 23) and 85th Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), member states of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) have been meeting informally to find a potential pathway for agreeing and adopting a robust set of policy measures capable of...
articles.body: New insight brief offers reflections on what is needed from shipping’s regulatory enforcement mechanism in International Shipping News 11/11/2026 In the run-up to the 23rd Intersessional Working Group (ISWG 23) and 85th Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85), member states of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) have been meeting informally to find a potential pathway for agreeing and adopting a robust set of policy measures capable of delivering on the IMO’s 2023 Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Strategy. Those informal meetings have led to several new design ideas about how companies could be required to comply with regulation. Discussions are ongoing, and the detail of any eventual proposal would need to be ironed out either in the legal text or in guidelines for implementation. The Getting to Zero Coalition has engaged with its member companies to better understand how business cases for decarbonisation, including zero- and near-zero (ZNZ) fuels, would be impacted by the alternative designs being discussed. At the time of writing, 15 member companies had been consulted, of which the majority were shipowners (container, dry bulk, and tanker all represented). Charterers, fuel producers, and infrastructure-side industry members were also consulted. The companies consulted were mostly based in Europe and Asia, with some participation from Latin American and US-based companies, but collective operational coverage from the 15 members is global. Mechanisms discussed with Getting to Zero Coalition members The companies discussed three scenarios, focusing on the enforcement mechanism and associated revenue flows for different mechanism types. Mechanisms discussed with Getting to Zero Coalition members The companies discussed three scenarios, focusing on the enforcement mechanism and associated revenue flows for different mechanism types. The first mechanism, the remedial unit, featured in the Net-Zero Framework (NZF) agreed at MEPC 83. The other two mechanisms are more recent proposals. These new proposals are framed as seeking political common ground, particularly around the economic element and the management of associated funds. Substantively, they propose to shift control over compliance outlays towards shipowners, which is presumed to promote more efficient use of funds and lower costs of the transition. The evaluation by member companies considered the extent to which these goals would be achieved, alongside impacts on the business case for investing in ZNZs. Key messages from Getting to Zero Coalition members Channelling revenue generated by non-compliance fees into projects chosen by shipowners, either as direct contributions or investments, would significantly weaken the compliance signal and would not deliver the fuel uptake or equity outcomes policymakers have committed to. Further, they seem unlikely to succeed on their own terms of efficacy and cost reduction. Companies interviewed emphasised four messages: 1. Keep the penalty real and simple (through the RU): returning money to shipowners by allowing non-compliance fees to be treated as investments dilutes the price signal and creates poor optics for industry. All companies consulted indicated the wish to keep the penalty a true and meaningful (and comparatively simple) penalty. 2. DCs and VUs are unlikely to lower costs: shipowners optimise over three months to one year, and the potential of future profits will not impact freight rates, which will rise just as much as they would under a simple penalty. 3. Governance and trust matters to the industry: for shipowners to trust that the system would not be abused such that it undermines any GHG mitigation action they take, extensive oversight and safeguards would be needed—essentially the same oversight and safeguards that would be needed for a fund or facility. 4. Contributions and investments will not solve the energy transition challenge or support equity: fuel producers need offtake, not funding, and shipowners directing revenues to certain projects or optimising for returns will not deliver a just and equitable transition on their own. 1.Keep the penalty real, and keep it simple A penalty only changes behaviour if its net cost to the payer stays high. Every company consulted said that returning the money through an investment significantly weakens the signal without delivering on other objectives. •VUs will weaken the incentive to switch fuels compared to RUs: Shipowners compare the cost of switching fuel against the cost of business as usual. If part of the penalty comes back as an investment return, the effective cost of non-compliance falls and the switch looks less urgent. •DCs and VUs increase the complexity for shipowners: The NZF was often criticised for its complexity. DCs and VUs only add more complexity, and shipowners prefer RU to DC and VU in part because they are simpler. The overall impacts and benefits of contributions and investments cannot be easily foreseen and therefore complicate companies’ compliance strategies. •VUs, in particular, generate a real reputational risk for the industry: Under this design, a firm pays a cost for not reducing emissions, which is then repaid through a return on some or all of those costs that form investments. This undermines the penalty’s credibility with the sector and the public, yet shipowners will be “forced” to play along to stay even with competitors. Consulted companies see the optics as poor and do not want to be put in this position by regulators. 2.VU investments will not move freight rates nor lower trade costs Based on interviewee responses, returns from VU investments will not allow shipowners to lower freight rates. Shipowners make fuel choices and set freight rates based on return timelines ranging from three months to a year. While the potential of future investment returns will weaken the incentive to adopt low-carbon fuels, those returns would have to be proven, stable, and predictable before they would potentially flow through to freight rates in a competitive market. All companies indicated that any returns from VUs would be treated as “the cherry on top of their balance sheets at the end of the year,” rather than a meaningful flow of financial support. Timing and accounting pose a core problem. The penalty is due at year-end, while the return comes at an uncertain later date, so it cannot be used to plan for or finance a fuel switch or a reduction of freight rates. 3.Trust and governance: the necessary safeguards would be the same as those required by a fund/facility •Shipowners interviewed did not fully trust the IMO to handle the money well, but they trust themselves and their competitors even less. Companies anticipate shipowner handling of direct contributions or investments to lead to fraud almost immediately. •Managing that risk would require oversight of project selection and scrutiny of returns. At that level of control, the arrangement ends up being close to what would be required for a fund or facility under the NZF. Yet instead of scrutinising a single fund led by public representatives, authorities would have to scrutinise individual companies, their projects, and their impacts. The business case suffers twice, with companies both carrying the administrative burden and losing the simplicity they had hoped for. 4.DCs and VUs will not solve the energy transition challenge or support equity While it’s not yet clear where DC or VU investments would go, the interviewees suggested that the best case (from the perspective of the IMO’s 2023 GHG strategy) would be for these to be targeted at ZNZ projects and investments in the most negatively impacted countries. However, even if the investments were to be targeted, interviewees expect their impact to be constrained. •Fuel producers need offtake, not funding: the most efficient way for fuel producers to raise finance is by securing offtake, rather than receiving funding without clear offtakes in sight. Furthermore, allowing shipowners to pick projects may disperse financing in ways that dilute the economies of scale needed to invest in fuel production. Driving cost-competitive scale in the ZNZ supply chain requires concentrating investment in fewer fuel production opportunities in the short term, which is unlikely to occur if shipowners select their projects individually. •Shipowners do not want to be held responsible for delivering a just and equitable transition: lower-income countries struggle to attract investment due to higher capital costs. However, allowing shipowners to direct their contributions will make investment in these countries less likely, as the consulted shipowners indicated they would not choose to take on these risks. Shipowners indicated that where they place contributions or investments would be tied to their home bases or operating routes, an outcome that could favour shipowning-heavy regions and undermine the level playing field. Some pointed to the possibility of stacking incentives, since investing in EU-based fuel production could unlock other EU funding. This would then favour regions that already have the capacity to support the transition. Even if forced to pick just and equitable transition-related projects, many companies are unfamiliar with those geographies, do not know local circumstances, and find follow-up difficult. •Trade costs would remain high, yet any support for low-income countries to offset this would be removed: as noted above, no freight rate effect from VUs is expected, so routes to lower-income countries would not benefit. Further, any future returns would be channelled into high-utilisation, high-competition routes such as Asia-Europe and Asia-North America. Lower-income countries are unlikely to see benefit from this. Source: Global Maritime Forum 2026-11-11 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

The company operates a fleet of remotely operated and lean-crewed vessels used for offshore surveys and subsea operations. One of its Armada vessels participated in Royal Navy trials earlier this year. The initial programme will also draw on UK technology suppliers, with much of the equipment expected to come from small and medium-sized businesses. articles.body: Interconnectors November 11, 2026 · 1 minute ago Main construction starts on central part of interconnection between Western Isles and UK NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email SSEN Transmission SSEN Transmission has started main construction of the Lewis Hub project, a central part of the interconnector that will link the Scottish Western Isles to the UK national electricity transmission network for the first time. The groundbreaking, which marks the project’s progression from initial site preparation into main construction, was held on November 5 at the Lewis Hub site at Arnish Moor near Stornoway. Lewis Hub will comprise a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) converter station and AC substation and will form a central part of the wider Western Isles HVDC Link. The 1.8 GW interconnector will consist of approximately 83 kilometers of underground cable and 81 kilometers of subsea cable, connecting the Lewis Hub HVDC converter station and AC substation on the Isle of Lewis to the mainland. In the same week the groundbreaking took place, Highlands-based civil engineering contractor RJ McLeod signed a contract to deliver the first major package of construction works that will prepare the site for the HVDC converter station, AC substation and associated infrastructure. “Breaking ground on the Lewis Hub is a hugely significant moment for the project and for the Western Isles. A direct connection between the Western Isles and the main GB transmission network has been an ambition for decades. Through the Lewis Hub and wider Western Isles Connection, we are now turning that ambition into reality, unlocking the islands’ vast renewable energy potential and strengthening the electricity network for generations to come," said Sandy Mactaggart , Director of Offshore Delivery at SSEN Transmission. “But our ambition is about much more than delivering new infrastructure. We want this investment to create a lasting legacy for the islands, supporting local infrastructure, developing skills and creating opportunities for local businesses, while working with key partners to find mutually beneficial solutions that support long-term economic growth." The Western Isles HVDC Link is a key component of SSEN Transmission’s planned £22 billion investment program to upgrade the north of Scotland’s electricity transmission grid. The Scottish Government Marine Directorate at the beginning of 2026 granted the variation to the existing marine license , approved in 2021, for the subsea cable link, greenlighting the needed increase in capacity. Hitachi Energy is delivering the HVDC converter stations for the project and NKT the power cable system . "We are proud to support SSEN Transmission by delivering the complete 525 kV HVDC power cable system, covering design, production, installation and testing across the onshore and offshore sections," NKT said. "This is the scale of infrastructure needed to turn renewable energy potential into a more secure and interconnected power system. We are proud to be part of Western Isles and look forward to the milestones ahead." According to SSEN Transmission, the Lewis Hub project is expected to support more than 70 apprenticeship and trainee opportunities and is already delivering wider benefits to the local community, with a £1.06 million (approximately €1.27 million) Lewis Hub Local Fund due to launch soon. Together with future local funds associated with proposed transmission projects in the Western Isles, the fund is expected to contribute to more than £5 million in community benefit funding, subject to the relevant projects securing consent and progressing to main construction. articles.body: Europe Tankers Monjasa seals biggest-ever fleet deal with five-tanker swoop Adis Ajdin November 11, 2026 0 489 1 minute read Monjasa Monjasa Danish bunker supplier and shipowner Monjasa has acquired five sister product tankers from Germany’s Bernhard Schulte in its largest-ever fleet deal, strengthening its marine fuels operations in West Africa. The Fredericia-based group has picked up five 2010- and 2011-built tankers of around 16,500 dwt each. The purchase price has not been disclosed. Four vessels, renamed Monjasa Tracer, Monjasa Tuner, Monjasa Twister and Monjasa Tracker , have already joined the fleet and are trading in West Africa and Northwest Europe. The fifth, Monjasa Trigger , is set to follow by the end of November. The ships previously traded as Eva Schulte, Erika Schulte, Everhard Schulte, Edzard Schulte and Elisabeth Schulte , respectively. The acquisition takes Monjasa’s owned fleet to 20 tankers, alongside around 10 ships on time charter. Group chief executive Anders Østergaard described the purchase as the company’s largest single tonnage acquisition, highlighting the benefits of taking on five identical vessels with established operating costs and technical requirements. “Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day,” he said. The tankers will initially support Monjasa’s West African operations, although the company also sees opportunities to employ them in commercial freight trading and elsewhere in its global supply network. The deal builds on Monjasa’s earlier tanker investments in West Africa, including the 2023 acquisition of the 68,589 dwt Monjasa Leader and the 13,051 dwt Monjasa Refiner , which were brought in for floating storage and bunker supply operations, respectively. The contract covers integrated subsurface, geomechanics and well engineering studies for the Viking East and Viking West storage sites. The work will assess storage capacity, geological containment and carbon dioxide injectivity, helping reduce technical risks associated with the project’s planned expansion. Harbour Energy is developing Viking CCS and holds a 60% operating interest, alongside BP with 40%. The project aims to transport and permanently store carbon dioxide captured from industrial facilities in the Humber region. Its initial phase is designed to store up to 4m tonnes of CO₂ annually from the early 2030s, with Harbour targeting capacity of up to 15m tonnes per year by 2035. The development plans to reuse existing southern North Sea infrastructure, including an offshore pipeline linking the former Theddlethorpe gas terminal to depleted Viking gas reservoirs approximately 2.7 km beneath the seabed. Viking completed front-end engineering design in 2025 and secured development consent for its onshore pipeline the same year. The project received approval for £65.5m ($87.3m) in UK government development funding in July 2026, with that support retained in the latest government budget. A final investment decision remains outstanding, with the latest engineering award intended to support further development of the project’s offshore storage capacity. articles.body: Exploration & Production November 11, 2026 · 9 minutes ago Ghana's oil & gas drilling yields hydrocarbons and first carbonate reservoir This hydrocarbon discovery in a carbonate reservoir off Ghana's coast is unlocking new potential for the country’s upstream sector. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPSO Kwame Nkrumah (for illustration purposes) Source: Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) A new discovery has been made at a deepwater exploration well off the coast of Ghana, marking the country's first successful test of a carbonate reservoir system and opening the door for a brand-new geological play that could help replenish dwindling reserves and attract fresh investment to the West African nation's energy industry. Planet One Oil & Gas , as the operator alongside its partners in the Deepwater Cape Three Points (DWCTP) Block , Ghana National Petroleum Corporation (GNPC) and GOIL Upstream , has discovered hydrocarbons at the Nya Gyidie-1X exploration well offshore Ghana. GNPC describes the result as an important development in the country's efforts to find new petroleum resources to sustain future production, as this discovery establishes a new geological target for further exploration, beyond the sandstone reservoirs associated with the country's existing commercial oil and gas fields. Located approximately 148 kilometers off the coast of Ghana, Nya Gyidie-1X, which was drilled in water depths of 2,289 meters, encountered hydrocarbons in carbonate rock between 3,364 and 3,499 meters measured depth along the wellbore. According to Ghana National Petroleum Corporation, the result is particularly encouraging for Ghana's upstream petroleum industry, where replacing produced reserves, attracting fresh exploration investment, and addressing declining production remain important priorities. " The significance of Nya Gyidie-1X goes beyond the hydrocarbons encountered in this well. For the first time in Ghana, we have tested and confirmed hydrocarbons in a carbonate reservoir system, opening up a new geological play for further exploration. At a time when replenishing our reserves and sustaining production are national priorities, this is an encouraging development. The next task is to establish the scale and commercial potential of the discovery through rigorous technical evaluation. GNPC looks forward to working with Planet One and GOIL Upstream to build on this result and advance the development and production opportunities it presents for Ghana. " — Kwame Ntow Amoah GNPC's Chief Executive Related Articles Fossil Energy Four more wells set to come online in months ahead offshore Ghana 3 min read The company emphasizes that this discovery is expected to help consolidate the renewed wave of interest and investment in petroleum exploration and production, with a particular focus on identifying additional resources and improving the upstream sector's long-term outlook. Further technical work is required to determine the size, characteristics, and commercial viability of this discovery to guide subsequent exploration and appraisal decisions. The partners and the relevant regulatory institutions will evaluate the discovery to determine the next steps. articles.summary: Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes....
articles.body: Dry Cargo Coal’s new world order takes shape Sam Chambers November 11, 2026 0 822 1 minute read Coal’s changing trade map is creating winners and losers across dry bulk shipping in 2026, with Indonesian exports retreating, southern African shipments setting records and Asian import demand increasingly fractured. Clarksons Research forecasts seaborne coal trade will edge up just 1% this year to 1.343bn tonnes. Beneath that modest increase, Indonesian exports are projected to fall 6% to 496.9m tonnes, while Australian shipments climb 4% to 371.3m tonnes. Chinese seaborne imports are expected to decline 5%, India’s 3%, while Japan’s rise 3%. The Indonesian retreat is already evident on loading lists. Braemar’s analysis of AXSMarine tracking shows exports falling 8% year-on-year during January-October. Capesize shipments were down 24%, supramax and ultramax movements 12%, and panamax cargoes 4%. Export procedures and low river levels have compounded pressure on shipments. Southern Africa presents a contrast. Ursa Shipbrokers calculates combined South African and Mozambican steam coal exports reached a ten-year high of 64.92m tonnes during January-October, with 27.26m tonnes destined for India. Globally, however, tracked seaborne steam coal trade fell 1.5% to 801.1m tonnes, including a 7.9% decline in Indonesian shipments. India offers perhaps the year’s biggest paradox. BIMCO reports coal imports dropped 7% in the first ten months despite coal-fired electricity generation rising around 9%. Expensive imported supplies have encouraged greater reliance on domestic production and stock drawdowns. BRS says coal inventories at power stations were equivalent to only 5.9 days of consumption, against 14.7 days a year earlier. Supramaxes have been hardest hit, with Indian-bound coal volumes falling 16%, compared with a 4% decline for panamaxes. October offered the first signs of a turn, with Indian seaborne coal arrivals rising 7% year-on-year. However, BIMCO expects only a limited import recovery in 2027 as domestic mining grows. The Middle East energy crisis has meanwhile encouraged coal-fired generation in parts of Europe and northeast Asia as LNG supplies tightened. The changing dynamics of global coal trades will come under the spotlight at Geneva Dry 2027 next April, where panellists, including Danilo Fumarola, CEO of Gestion Maritime Group, and Peter Weernink, chairman of SwissMarine, will examine shifting tonne-mile patterns, the routes gaining ground, China’s appetite for coal imports and whether the fallout from the war around the Strait of Hormuz will have a lasting impact on demand.
